title: Segmenting Words into Sounds
keyIdea: To spell a word, say it slowly and split it into its sounds. This is called segmenting. Give each sound its own box, then write the letter or letters for that sound: c-a-t, cat. Count sounds, not letters, so ship has 3 boxes (sh-i-p). Listen for the vowel sound in the middle, and in words like frog and tent, hear both sounds that sit side by side.

kid: Blending is for reading. Segmenting is for spelling. To spell sun, say it slowly. Stretch it like a rubber band: s … u … n. That is three sounds.
Draw a box for each sound. Then write the letter for each sound in its box. s in the first box, u in the next, n in the last. Now you have sun.
Some sounds need two letters. In ship, sh is one sound. It goes in one box. So ship has 4 letters but 3 boxes: sh, i, p.
Do not lose a sound. The middle sound is easy to miss: cat needs its a. In frog, f and r sit side by side. Say it slowly and you hear both: f … r … o … g.
adult: Segmenting means splitting a spoken word into its phonemes (sounds) so a child can write a grapheme for each one. It is the spelling twin of blending, and English National Curriculum Year 1 expects children to spell words containing each of the 40+ phonemes taught by segmenting them. The US Common Core asks the same in L.K.2d and L.1.2e: spell simple words phonetically, drawing on phoneme-grapheme knowledge.

Sound boxes (Elkonin boxes) make the sounds visible: one box per phoneme, never one per letter. A digraph such as sh, ch or ck, or a double letter such as gg in egg, shares one box. Adjacent consonants, often called blends or consonant clusters (fr, st, nd), are two phonemes and need two boxes. CVC words come first, then CCVC and CVCC words such as frog, stop and hand.

Common mistakes: leaving out the medial vowel (ct for cat), dropping the second sound of a cluster (fog for frog, sop for stop), splitting a digraph across two boxes (s-h for sh), and writing letter names instead of sounds. Be careful to say pure sounds, mmm not muh, because an added uh sound makes children write extra letters.

In the lab your child picks the strip with one box per sound, drops the vowel into an empty middle box, puts back the lost sound in a blend, and spells whole words with tiles where sh, ck and ch fill one box. Every drag has a big button twin.

familyTip: Play 'robot talk' at tea time. Say a word in sounds, like c … u … p, and ask your child to say the word. Then swap: they say a word in sounds for you. Tap one finger for each sound to count them.

visual.caption: How many sounds? Drag each word to the right number of sound boxes, or tap it and then tap a group.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: count the sounds, fill the middle box, put back lost sounds, and spell words in sound boxes.

practice.hint: Say it slowly and tap a finger for each sound.
practice.explain: h … e … n. Three sounds, so three boxes.

practice.prompt: Zara spells {a} words. Each word has 3 sounds. How many sound boxes does she draw?
practice.hint: Each word needs 3 boxes. Add 3 for every word.
practice.explain: {a} words with 3 boxes each make {=3*a} boxes.

practice.prompt: Which spelling of “stop” has every sound?
practice.hint: Stretch it: s … t … o … p. Is every sound there?
practice.explain: s and t sit side by side, and you hear both. sop and top each lose a sound.

practice.prompt: A word has {n} letters. Two of them are sh, which makes one sound. Every other letter makes its own sound. How many sound boxes?
practice.hint: sh fills one box, not two. Take one away from the letters.
practice.explain: {n} letters, but sh shares one box, so {=n-1} boxes. Fish: 4 letters, 3 boxes.

pool.prompt: Tom writes “bd” for bed. What did he miss?
pool.hint: Say bed slowly. What comes between b and d?
pool.explain: b … e … d. The middle vowel sound e was lost.

pool.prompt: How many sound boxes does “duck” need?
pool.hint: ck makes one sound. It goes in one box.
pool.explain: d … u … ck. Four letters, but three sounds.

pool.prompt: What is the first sound in “ship”?
pool.hint: Say it slowly. Do you hear s, or a shush sound?
pool.explain: s and h together make one sound, sh. Write sh in the first box.

pool.hint: Tap a finger for each sound you hear.
pool.explain: f … r … o … g is four sounds. fog and dog have three.

pool.prompt: What is the last sound in “hand”?
pool.hint: Say hand slowly and listen to the very end.
pool.explain: h … a … n … d. n and d sit side by side, and d comes last.

pool.prompt: Which sound goes in the middle box of “pig”?
pool.hint: Stretch it: p … ? … g. Is it i as in ink?
pool.explain: p … i … g. With e it would say peg, and with a it would say pag.

pool.prompt: Each word on a card has 4 sounds. There are {a} cards. How many sound boxes in all?
pool.hint: Each card needs 4 boxes. Count in fours.
pool.explain: {a} cards with 4 boxes each make {=4*a} boxes.

pool.prompt: Ben says the letter names “see, ay, tee”. What should he write for cat?
choices: A letter for each name, seeaytee
pool.hint: In a word, we write the sound, not the letter name.
pool.explain: Say the sounds, not the names: c … a … t. One letter for each sound.

pool.prompt: A word has {n} letters and ends in ck, which makes one sound. Every other letter makes its own sound. How many sound boxes?
pool.hint: c and k share one box at the end. Take one away from the letters.
pool.explain: {n} letters, but ck fills one box, so {=n-1} boxes. Duck: 4 letters, 3 boxes.
